Bereft

/bih-REFT/ - rhymes with left · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Bereft means devoid of, without.

With both children settled overseas, the holidays left the couple feeling bereft, the table too big and the house too quiet.

Worked Example

The village lost its bus route in the spring cuts, and by autumn people spoke of being bereft of far more than transport: the 7:40 had been where engagements were announced, gossip settled, and quarrels patched up.

Bereft is sharper than plain 'without' because it carries the ache of having once had the thing. It is the old past form of 'bereave' — to be bereft is literally to have been robbed, and the word keeps that sense of felt, personal loss.

How Bereft Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

deprived

deprived: something was withheld or taken — the focus is on the taking

devoid

devoid: simply empty of a thing, with no feeling of loss attached

Antonyms

endowed

endowed: richly supplied with a gift or quality

brimming

brimming: full to overflowing

How Strong Is It? — lacking → deprived → bereft

lacking vs. bereft

lacking vs. bereft: Lacking is far milder than bereft — a report can be lacking in detail without anyone grieving over it.

deprived vs. bereft

deprived vs. bereft: Deprived is weaker than bereft — it notes that something was withheld or taken, without the aching sense of loss that bereft carries.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — be-

Prefix — be-: thoroughly, away

Root — reft

Root — reft: robbed (past form of Old English reafian, to plunder)

Put it together

Put it together: Be- (thoroughly) + reft (robbed) = thoroughly robbed. Bereft is the fossilized past form of bereave: Old English reafian meant to plunder, and someone bereft has been plundered of what they loved — the word never forgets that what is missing was once theirs.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: The robber verb inside bereft — Old English reafian, 'to plunder' — dropped out of everyday English centuries ago, so there is no common cousin left to find. Only its own siblings survive: bereave, and bereaved for those the robbery of death has visited.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Bereft is for the felt absence of something once possessed — bereft of hope, of company, of purpose — and it usually keeps its preposition: bereft OF. Plain 'without' states a fact; bereft mourns it. Beside its unit-mates: forlorn looks abandoned and abject is degraded, but bereft always points at the particular treasure that is gone.
